claims.text: Controlled annealing can direct phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Controlled annealing promotes equilibrium phase formation from a metastable state.
The initial alloy may have a metastable as-cast or rapidly cooled microstructure containing non-equilibrium phases.
An isothermal hold at a target temperature followed by controlled cooling can be used as the annealing regime.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation during annealing.
Annealing enhances atomic diffusion along grain boundaries and through the bulk.
Enhanced diffusion promotes nucleation and growth of equilibrium phases.
Heat treatment increases atomic mobility and facilitates diffusional reordering from non-equilibrium to equilibrium phases.
Heat treatment reduces energy barriers for precipitation and coarsening.
Precipitation and coarsening lead to a stabilized phase distribution.
Controlled annealing produces a reproducible microstructure with refined and controlled phase composition.
The annealed microstructure has improved or more predictable mechanical properties than the initial state.
The untreated alloy has a heterogeneous, metastable mixture of non-equilibrium phases resulting from rapid cooling.
The effectiveness of annealing is limited by the selected temperature and duration.
Kinetic hindrances and batch-to-batch compositional inhomogeneity may alter annealing effectiveness.
Phase-transformation pathways may vary with composition and processing history.

contradictions.description: The mechanism invokes coarsening, whereas the outcome asserts a refined microstructure without explaining how coarsening produces refinement.

The predicted outcome allows mechanical properties to be either improved or merely predictable, but the falsification rule treats failure to improve mechanical properties as falsifying the hypothesis.
